# Sparse Voxel DAGs

Also called: SVDAG, Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph

## Overview
Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAGs) are hierarchical data structures that represent 3D voxel grids as directed acyclic graphs by merging identical subtrees into shared nodes, thereby reducing memory footprint compared to standard tree structures like Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) [S1][S2]. While SVOs efficiently encode empty regions, they store redundant copies of identical non-empty geometry; SVDAGs solve this by allowing nodes to share pointers to identical subtrees, achieving compression ratios of 1 to 3 orders of magnitude in node count [S2]. This family sets itself apart from siblings by explicitly decoupling the geometric hierarchy from the storage of material attributes and by employing various strategies (bottom-up reduction, pointerless encoding, or hash-based recycling) to identify and merge isomorphic structures [S1][S2].

## Shared principles
All structures in this family share the following mechanism:

1.  **Recursive Subdivision:** The 3D domain is recursively divided into sub-volumes. In standard octrees, each node has 8 children. In pointer trees, the branching factor $N$ varies ($N^3$ children).
2.  **Sparsity Encoding:** Empty regions are represented by null pointers or absence of children, rather than storing zero-valued voxels. This provides compression proportional to the sparsity of the data.
3.  **Hierarchical Traversal:** Rendering or access requires traversing from the root to the leaf. This allows skipping large empty volumes (culling) and adapting resolution to view distance or detail requirements.
4.  **Spatial Locality:** Children of a node are spatially contiguous. This locality is often exploited via Morton ordering (Z-order curve) to map 3D coordinates to 1D keys, enabling efficient neighbor lookups and linear array representations in implicit variants [G].
5.  **Subtree Merging:** The core differentiator of the DAG family is the identification of structurally identical subtrees (isomorphic nodes) and their replacement with a single shared instance. This transforms the tree topology into a graph where multiple parents may reference the same child node, eliminating redundancy [S1][S2].

## Subtopics

### [Bottom-up SVO to DAG Reduction](898-bottom-up-svo-to-dag-reduction.md)
This method reduces the memory footprint of a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by identifying and merging identical subtrees into shared nodes, thereby transforming the tree structure into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). While an SVO efficiently encodes empty regions of space, it stores redundant copies of identical non-empty geometry. This method solves that inefficiency by allowing nodes to share pointers to identical subtrees, achieving compression ratios of 1 to 3 orders of magnitude in node count. It sets itself apart from top-down recursive merging by using an iterative bottom-up approach, which is computationally efficient and guarantees finding the minimal DAG within $L$ iterations, where $L$ is the maximum tree level. See [Bottom-up SVO to DAG Reduction](898-bottom-up-svo-to-dag-reduction.md).

### [Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG)](949-pointerless-sparse-voxel-directed-acyclic-graph-psvdag.md)
The Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG) is a hierarchical data structure that represents a 3D voxel grid as a directed acyclic graph without using explicit pointers to child nodes. It solves the problem of memory efficiency in sparse volume representation by combining the Common Subtree Merging (CSM) capabilities of Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAGs) with the space-saving benefits of pointerless encoding. Unlike standard SVDAGs, which rely on fixed-width pointers, PSVDAG uses variable-length binary labels and callers to reference shared subtrees, achieving higher compression ratios at the cost of traversal speed. It is particularly suited for archiving and streaming due to its compact binary representation, though it supports conversion to SVDAGs for faster access. See [Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG)](949-pointerless-sparse-voxel-directed-acyclic-graph-psvdag.md).

### [Sparse Voxel DAG Ray Traversal](1147-sparse-voxel-dag-ray-traversal.md)
Sparse Voxel DAG (SVDAG) ray traversal is a GPU-based method for efficiently traversing a compressed sparse voxel representation to perform visibility queries (shadows, ambient occlusion) and primary ray intersection. It builds on [Sparse Voxel DAGs](2791-sparse-voxel-dags.md) by exploiting node sharing to reduce memory footprint while maintaining traversal performance comparable to standard Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs). Unlike standard SVO traversal, it must handle potential cycles in the graph structure by tracking visited nodes, but avoids complex intersection tests with contours. See [Sparse Voxel DAG Ray Traversal](1147-sparse-voxel-dag-ray-traversal.md).

### [Isomorphic Node Recycling (DAOG)](3422-isomorphic-node-recycling-daog.md)
Isomorphic Node Recycling is a compression method that converts a standard Sparse Voxel Octree into a Directed Acyclic Octal Graph (DAOG) by reusing structurally identical (isomorphic) nodes. Unlike standard octrees where every node is a distinct memory object, this method identifies nodes with identical child structures or leaf values and merges them into a single shared instance, reducing memory footprint. It is distinguished from [Bottom-up SVO to DAG Reduction](898-bottom-up-svo-to-dag-reduction.md) by its top-down, hash-based insertion strategy during construction, and from [Pointerless Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graph (PSVDAG)](949-pointerless-sparse-voxel-directed-acyclic-graph-psvdag.md) by its reliance on a hash table for structural equality checks rather than implicit indexing. See [Isomorphic Node Recycling (DAOG)](3422-isomorphic-node-recycling-daog.md).

### [BasicDAG](6740-basicdag.md)
BasicDAG is a sparse voxel directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure that stores node indices in a flat, contiguous array to enable fast, cache-friendly traversal and leaf extraction. It differs from sibling variants by decoupling the geometric DAG structure from color data storage strategies, relying on a simple static array layout for node indexing rather than complex pointer trees or hash maps. See [BasicDAG](6740-basicdag.md).

### Aokana
Streaming/LOD variant of DAG that splits the world into many shallow DAGs of 256³ Voxels each, with octree-style LOD levels (LOD n is 8 children merged at the same 256³ resolution) and distance-based streaming [S1]. On an RTX 3060 Ti it renders a 64K scene of about 10 billion Voxels in about 6 ms. Only about 2–17% of the data is resident: 424 MB VRAM against 23 GB on disk for San Miguel at 64K [S1]. In Aokana's numbers, colour dominates storage: 21 GB of colour against 2.2 GB of geometry [S1]. Game attributes cannot utilize complex lossy compression [S1].

## Background
The concept of Directed Acyclic Graphs in voxel representation emerged as a solution to the redundancy inherent in tree-based structures. While Octrees and Pointer Trees provide efficient sparsity encoding, they duplicate memory for identical geometric structures. The bottom-up reduction technique, which guarantees a minimal DAG, was developed to address this inefficiency [S1][S2]. Subsequent variants like PSVDAG and DAOG introduced alternative mechanisms for node sharing, such as pointerless binary encoding and hash-based isomorphism detection, to further optimize storage for streaming and archival purposes [S1, S2]. Recent applications, such as Aokana, have integrated DAGs into real-time rendering pipelines, demonstrating their viability for large-scale, high-resolution voxel scenes in interactive graphics [S1].
